Arabic SEO in Qatar: How to Rank in Both Arabic and English Search

by Glimpse Qatar | September 17, 2026

People in Qatar search in Arabic and in English, and often the same person uses both depending on the topic. Arabic is the official language, English is widely used in business, and the population is very international. A site that ranks in only one language is invisible to part of its market. Ranking in both takes more than translation. It takes separate research, a clean technical setup and content that reads as if it was written for the person searching.

Research keywords in each language separately

Translating your English keyword list into Arabic is the most common mistake in bilingual SEO. People do not search in translation. They search in the words they use every day.

  • Start from Arabic, not from English. Ask an Arabic-speaking researcher to list how customers describe your product, then check those terms in your keyword tools and in Google Search Console.

  • Expect spelling variants. Arabic queries vary with and without hamza on the alef, with taa marbuta or haa at the end of a word, and with different ways of writing foreign brand names in Arabic script. Group these variants and make sure your pages reflect the most common forms naturally.

  • Account for formal and everyday language. Modern Standard Arabic suits most website copy, but searchers may use Gulf dialect words for everyday products and services. Your research should show which is used for your category.

  • Look for mixed queries. Some users type an English brand or product name with Arabic words around it, or write Arabic words in Latin letters. Check whether these appear in your own search data before building content around them.

  • Add place names. Doha, Lusail, The Pearl, West Bay, Msheireb and Al Wakrah have Arabic and English forms. Use both in the relevant language version.

Give each language its own URLs

Search engines need a separate, crawlable page for each language. Avoid setups where the language changes through a cookie or script while the URL stays the same.

  • Use a clear structure such as /ar/ and /en/ folders, with every important page available in both.

  • Do not redirect users automatically based on location or browser language. Show a visible language switcher that links to the equivalent page, not back to the home page.

  • Translate URLs, titles, meta descriptions, image alt text and structured data, not only the body copy.

  • Keep internal links inside each language. An Arabic page should link to Arabic pages.

Set up hreflang correctly

Hreflang tells search engines which version of a page is meant for which language and region. For a Qatar-focused bilingual site, the usual values are ar-QA for Arabic and en-QA for English.

  • Every page should list all of its language versions, including itself.

  • The references must be reciprocal. If the English page points to the Arabic page, the Arabic page must point back.

  • Add an x-default value for users who match neither version.

  • If you also run sites for other Gulf countries, use hreflang across them so the Qatar pages appear for searchers in Qatar.

  • Make sure canonical tags point to the page's own language version. A canonical from the Arabic page to the English one tells search engines to ignore the Arabic page.

Check the setup after every site release. Hreflang errors are easy to introduce and rarely visible to the people browsing the site.

Build a proper right-to-left experience

Right-to-left layout matters for Arabic readers, and a poor experience undermines both rankings and conversions. Set the language and direction attributes on the Arabic pages, then check the details:

  • Navigation, breadcrumbs, sliders and progress indicators should mirror.

  • Icons that imply direction, such as arrows, should flip. Logos and media controls should not.

  • Choose a web font designed for Arabic, with comfortable line height. Arabic set in a font built for Latin text is hard to read.

  • Test forms, including phone number fields, error messages and confirmation emails.

Write Arabic content, do not convert it

Machine-translated pages are easy to spot. They use unnatural phrasing, miss the terms people search for and rarely earn links or shares. Brief an Arabic writer with the topic, the audience and the target terms, and let them write the page.

Useful formats for both languages include service pages for each location you serve, answers to common buyer questions, pricing and process explanations, and comparison guides. Clear question-and-answer content also helps you appear in AI-generated answers, which draw on well-structured pages.

Do the local SEO work in both languages

Google Business Profile matters for local search. Complete every field, choose accurate categories, add your business name and description in the form customers expect, and keep hours current during Ramadan and public holidays. Make sure your name, address and phone number match across your website, profile and directory listings. Reply to reviews in the language the customer used. If reviews are a weak point, a structured reputation management process will help more than any technical fix.

Measure each language on its own

  • Segment Google Search Console by the /ar/ and /en/ folders to see impressions, clicks and queries for each.

  • Track enquiries, calls and WhatsApp clicks by language version.

  • Review Arabic queries monthly with someone who reads Arabic. Reports filtered by a non-speaker miss patterns.

  • Support priority terms with paid search while organic rankings build, and use the paid data to refine your keyword list.

A short checklist

  • Separate Arabic and English keyword research completed

  • One URL per language per page, with a visible switcher

  • Reciprocal hreflang with ar-QA, en-QA and x-default

  • Self-referencing canonicals

  • Right-to-left layout tested on mobile

  • Arabic content written by a native writer

  • Google Business Profile complete and current

  • Reporting split by language
